The structures in the diagram are the subject of a large literature on planet populations. The gap in the radius distribution of small planets between super-Earths and sub-Neptunes \cite{fulton2017the,fulton2018the,eylen2018an} has been explained by photoevaporation \cite{owen2013kepler,owen2017the} and by core-powered mass loss \cite{ginzburg2018corepowered}, and the scarcity of Neptune-sized planets on short orbits has been described as a desert in the period-mass and period-radius planes \cite{szabo2011a,mazeh2016dearth,lundkvist2016hot,owen2018photoevaporation}. These studies work with samples of transiting planets with homogeneous radii and with explicit treatment of completeness; we do neither. Our paper does not test any explanation of these features. It asks a prior question about the archive table itself: which of its radii are measured and which follow from a mass-radius relation. We do not claim that the literature lacks such a tabulation; we provide it as a reproducible reference for the version of the archive we used. The terms ``calculated'' and ``mass-derived'' denote the same radii, and we use ``calculated'' because it is the archive's term.
